About

A voice between two landscapes

Shanza Mumtaz
Kallar Kahar, Punjab

I am Shanza Mumtaz, a Pakistani poet and literary writer from Kallar Kahar, Punjab, and a final-year Computer Engineering student at UET Taxila. Growing up in the Salt Range shaped my deep connection with nature, landscape, family, memory, and local traditions. My writing explores how places shape identity and how landscapes, traditions, and memories change alongside modern technology.

My work includes poetry, short fiction, nature writing, literary essays, and English-to-Urdu translation. My four book-length projects — The Geography of Silence, Where the Salt Hills Remember, Letters from the Lake, and the ongoing The Lake and the Circuit — reflect my interest in preserving the emotional and cultural histories of changing places.

Current Project

The Lake and the Circuit

A collection of essays that set the fixed, ancient landscape of the Salt Range against the fast, iterative logic of the machines I have spent four years learning to build — asking what a lake remembers, what a circuit forgets, and what it means to belong fully to neither.

Click any essay to read it in full.

Essay No. 01

Learning to Swim, Learning to Debug

Technology · MemoryWritten January 2023

The first time I went into Kallar Kahar Lake, I did not swim so much as fail, repeatedly, in the direction of not drowning. My cousins had already learned — they cut through the water like they'd been born knowing how, while I flailed, swallowed a mouthful of something brackish and green, and came up furious. My uncle, standing waist-deep, did not rescue me. He said, try again, but move your arms like this — and demonstrated, badly, from the shore. I tried again. I still sank. I tried a third time, adjusting some small thing I couldn't name, and for four strokes, I did not sink.

Years later, in a computer lab in Taxila, I would recognize that exact feeling — the fourth stroke, the not-sinking — hunched over a program that refused, for six straight hours, to run. Code is unforgiving in a way water is not: water, at least, holds you up a little, even when you're bad at it. Code gives you nothing. It simply returns an error, flat and indifferent, and expects you to find the one misplaced bracket, the one variable you forgot to define, somewhere in four hundred lines you already believed were correct.

What nobody tells you, about either lake or code, is that the failure is not separate from the skill — it is the skill, still forming. Each time I sank in that lake, my body was learning something my mind hadn't caught up to yet. Each time my program failed, some quiet part of my thinking was recalibrating, even while the conscious part of me wanted to throw the laptop into a body of water very much like that lake.

My uncle never once told me I was doing it right. He only ever said try again. I think now that this was the most useful sentence anyone taught me before I turned twelve — more useful, in its way, than anything I would later learn about loops or logic gates, because it was the sentence underneath all of it. Debugging is just swimming that you do sitting down. The lake is patient. The compiler is not. But both of them, eventually, if you keep adjusting that one small thing you can't yet name, will let you through.

Essay No. 02

The Lake in Winter

LandscapeWritten February 2023

By December, Kallar Kahar Lake goes quiet in a way that unsettles visitors and comforts locals. The boats are pulled in. The peacocks that strut for tourists in warmer months disappear into the tree line, and the water itself takes on a flat, pewter stillness, as if it has decided, for a season, to stop performing.

I used to think stillness meant nothing was happening. I know better now. Beneath that flat surface, the lake is doing what it always does — holding its minerals in suspension, keeping its temperature, waiting out the cold the way it has waited out every winter since Babur passed through and wrote of it in his memoirs. Nothing about the lake in winter is idle. It is simply patient in a register too slow for a passing glance to register.

I think of this every time I sit, blocked, in front of an assignment I cannot start. There is a kind of guilt that comes with visible non-productivity — the sense that if my hands aren't moving, nothing is being built. But some of my best solutions have arrived exactly the way spring arrives at the lake: not from effort applied in that moment, but from something that had been quietly working underneath the whole time.

My grandmother used to say winter is when the land does its thinking. I didn't understand her until I watched myself stare at a screen for three hours, accomplish nothing visible, and then solve the entire problem in the shower the next morning. The lake taught me this first, though I didn't know I was being taught. Some seasons are for freezing. Some are for thawing. Very few of them look like progress from the shore.

Essay No. 03

What the Hills Don't Compute

Landscape · TechnologyWritten March 2023

The Salt Range predates almost everything I know how to measure. Its rock is Precambrian in places — older than complex life, older than the concept of a year. When I studied computer science, I learned to think in units that would embarrass this landscape: a processor cycle lasts a fraction of a nanosecond; a framework I learned in my second year was "legacy" by my fourth.

There is something almost violent about that mismatch when you notice it. I grew up walking hills that have not meaningfully changed in longer than human language has existed, and then went to a university where an entire technology could rise and become obsolete within a single degree program.

I don't think the hills are indifferent to this, exactly — I think they simply operate on a timescale that renders indifference and attention equally irrelevant. A hill does not have opinions about being ignored. It has geology. And there is something I have started to envy in that: an existence not measured by how quickly it updates.

I am not arguing that we should abandon what moves fast. I like what moves fast — it's why I chose this degree, why I like the feeling of a program finally compiling. But I think growing up beneath something so old changes how you hold the fast things. You stop mistaking speed for permanence. The hills don't compute, and they don't need to. They were finished being impressive long before anyone arrived to measure them.

Essay No. 04

Salt in the Ground

LandscapeWritten April 2023

The Range is named for what's buried in it. Somewhere beneath Kallar Kahar's soil, and more famously beneath nearby Khewra, lies one of the largest salt deposits on Earth — laid down by an ocean that stopped existing millions of years before anyone was around to miss it. You can find salt crystallized pink in the local shops, carved into lamps, sold to tourists as souvenirs of something that used to be water.

I find it strange, and a little moving, that the most permanent thing about my home used to be liquid. Salt is what's left after everything else evaporates — the mineral record of a disappearance. It doesn't dissolve into nothing; it just waits, patient and crystalline, for the next thing to pass through it and pick some of it back up.

I think about this when I think about inheritance — not money, but the things that get passed down whether or not anyone means to pass them: a way of speaking, a habit of worry, my mother's particular silence when she disagrees with something. These things don't announce themselves as heirlooms. They just remain, embedded, long after whatever produced them has evaporated.

Engineering taught me to distrust anything I can't trace to a clear cause. But salt doesn't work that way, and neither, I've realized, do people. Some things are simply what's left. You don't have to understand the ocean to taste what it left behind.

Essay No. 05

Signal and Static

Technology · MemoryWritten April 2023

For most of my childhood, electricity in Kallar Kahar arrived on its own schedule, not ours. Load-shedding meant the fan would stop mid-spin at 9 p.m. without ceremony, and my mother kept candles in a drawer the way other households keep spare batteries — always within reach, never discussed.

What I remember most, though, isn't the darkness. It's what happened in it. Without a television running, without a phone to check, conversation filled the space instead — my grandmother telling the same three stories she always told, my cousins arguing about nothing, someone always eventually laughing too loud in the dark. The static of a bad signal, it turned out, was often better company than the show it interrupted.

When I got to university and studied networks properly — packets, bandwidth, the actual architecture of how information travels — I kept returning to this: connection was never really about signal strength. My village had terrible signal for years and somehow never had trouble connecting to itself. Meanwhile, I've sat in rooms full of perfect Wi-Fi where everyone was still, unmistakably, alone.

I don't romanticize the outages — they were genuinely inconvenient, and I don't miss ruined evenings of unfinished homework. But I think something got lost when the power stabilized and the phones came out. Static used to force us toward each other. Now the signal is strong enough that we no longer have to try.

Essay No. 06

My Father's Postings

Family · MemoryWritten May 2023

My father is a soldier, which meant that for most of my childhood, home was a place he returned to rather than a place he lived. Cantonments changed. Cities changed. What stayed fixed was Kallar Kahar — the one coordinate that didn't move while everything else did.

I used to resent this a little, the way children resent absences they don't yet have language for. It took me longer than it should have to understand that his postings weren't chosen for their convenience to us; they were orders, and orders don't negotiate with a daughter's school calendar. What I understand now, that I didn't then, is that his discipline — the folded uniforms, the exact hours, the refusal to complain about any of it — was its own kind of love letter to us, written in the only dialect he had: reliability, delivered from wherever he happened to be stationed.

There's a particular kind of engineering in a military family, though no one calls it that. Systems for staying in touch before smartphones. Contingencies for his absence during Eid, exams, emergencies. My mother ran that system without ever naming it a system. I only recognized the architecture of it once I started building actual ones — redundancy, fallback plans, a single source of truth everyone could return to.

That source of truth, in our case, was never a location. It was the fact that he always came back, eventually, to the same hills. I think that's the real definition of home for an army family — not a fixed address, but a fixed person you can locate any distance from.

Essay No. 07

My Mother's Hands

FamilyWritten June 2023

My mother has never used the word "system" to describe what she does, but I don't know a better one. Watch her cook for a joint family gathering and you are watching someone execute, from memory, a process with more moving parts than most of the software I've been taught to design — timing four dishes to finish within minutes of each other, adjusting for who's arrived, who's running late, who doesn't eat what, all without a whiteboard, a plan, or a single visible moment of doubt.

I spent years assuming this kind of work was simple because it was invisible — because no one called it a skill, because there was no certificate for it, because she herself would wave it off if asked. It took studying actual systems, actual algorithms, for me to recognize what I'd been watching my whole life: loops, conditionals, error handling, all executed by hand, in a kitchen, without a single line of it ever being written down.

Her hands know things mine don't. They know exactly how much give a dough needs before kneading becomes overworking. They know, without a thermometer, when oil is ready. This is a form of expertise nobody made her sit exams for, and it will not appear on any resume, including her own.

I don't want to overstate the comparison — her work and mine are not the same, and I don't think she'd thank me for flattening the difference. But I recognize the shape of what she does now in a way I couldn't as a child. Precision. Repetition. A refusal to let anything fail quietly. I think I learned to debug at her elbow, years before I ever touched a keyboard.

Essay No. 08

Terraces

Landscape · FamilyWritten July 2023

The hills around Kallar Kahar are cut, in places, into terraces — narrow shelves of farmable land carved into slopes too steep to plant otherwise. Nobody living remembers who built the first one. They were simply inherited, the way a language is inherited, adjusted slightly by each generation that used them and then passed whole to the next.

There's a kind of design intelligence in a terrace that took me a long time to see, because it doesn't announce itself as intelligence. It looks, at first, like just a shape in a hillside. But it's solving a real problem — how to hold soil and water on a slope that would otherwise simply wash away — and it's been solving that problem, without revision, for longer than any codebase I've ever touched has existed.

I think about "legacy systems" differently now. In engineering, legacy usually means outdated — something we tolerate until we can replace it with something more elegant. But a terrace is legacy in the other sense: something proven exactly because it has not needed replacing. Nobody has found a more elegant way to farm that hillside in generations, because the terrace already solved it.

I don't think this means old solutions are always right, or that new ones are always suspect. But I've started to notice how much of what I was taught to call innovation is really just rediscovery, dressed in different material. Somewhere on that hillside is a shape my ancestors got right the first time, and I am only now, with considerably more formal training, arriving at the same answer.

Essay No. 09

Night Sky Without Streetlights

Landscape · TechnologyWritten August 2023

Before the wider roads came, before the motorway made Kallar Kahar easy to reach, the town went properly dark at night — no streetlamp glow to compete with, no headlights passing steadily enough to matter. On clear nights, the sky above the lake did something I have never once seen replicated in a city: it went genuinely, densely full, the Milky Way visible as an actual band rather than a phrase from a poem.

I didn't understand, as a child, that this was rare. I assumed every sky looked like that until I went to Taxila for university and looked up one night out of habit, expecting the same fullness, and found instead a scattering — a dozen stars, maybe, competing with sodium light and a haze I hadn't noticed until its absence had something to contrast against.

Development is not a villain in this story. The roads that dimmed my sky also brought a hospital within reach, cut a six-hour drive to two, made my father's postings easier to bear. I'm not interested in an essay that simply mourns progress from a place of comfort I only have because of it.

But I think it's worth saying plainly what gets traded, even in a fair trade: I got infrastructure, and I lost a sky. Both of those are true at once, and I don't think the ledger balances as neatly as either side wants to claim. Some nights, visiting home, I still walk to the edge of town, past the last working streetlamp, just to see how much is still there. Some of it is. Not all of it.

Essay No. 10

Returning

Memory · LandscapeWritten September 2023

There is a specific bend in the road, coming from the motorway, where Kallar Kahar first becomes visible below — the lake catching light before anything else does, the hills arranging themselves into the shape I have measured every other landscape against since I was old enough to compare things. I have driven past that bend more times than I can count, and it has never once failed to do something to my chest.

I used to think leaving for university would be the story — the girl from the small town who went and studied circuits and code, who left the lake for something faster. But four years in, I've realized the leaving was never the actual story. The story is what happens at the bend in the road, every time I come back: the specific, involuntary way the landscape still claims me, no matter how much I've learned to build in the meantime.

I don't think I'll stay in engineering and abandon this place, the way certain narratives about "escaping" a small town seem to require. I think I'll do both, badly and imperfectly, the way most people do most things — carry the hills into rooms that have never heard of them, and carry the circuits back to a lake that doesn't need them and never asked for them.

What the lake taught me, in the end, wasn't patience or stillness or any of the tidy lessons I reached for earlier in this collection. It taught me that you can leave a place completely and still, at one particular bend in one particular road, discover you never actually left at all.

Essay No. 11

Where the View Changes All at Once

LandscapeWritten September 2023

There is a bend on the road above the lake — just past the old forest rest house, where the track narrows and the eucalyptus close in on both sides — where the whole valley arrives at once. You are walking through trees, hearing only your own feet, and then you are not. The land drops away and the lake is suddenly there, flat and pewter-colored, ringed by the hills like something set down carefully inside them. I have walked that bend hundreds of times and it has never once failed to surprise me.

I used to think this was a fact about the geography — that the trees hid the view and the bend revealed it, simple as a curtain. Now I think it is a fact about attention. The view was always there, at every point along the path, if you climbed the slope and looked. What the bend does is force the looking. It removes the choice.

I have spent four years learning systems that reveal themselves gradually, one function call at a time, no surprises if you read carefully enough. The bend has taught me to distrust that comfort a little. Some things you cannot debug your way toward. You have to walk until the trees run out.

The road is still there, and the bend, and the eucalyptus doing their slow work of concealment. I drive it now with people who have never seen the lake, and I have learned to say nothing before the corner — to let the geography do what it does. Their sharp intake of breath when the water opens up is, I have decided, one of the few renewable resources my hometown produces. Some views you get tired of. This one I have watched arrive a hundred times, and it has not once arrived the same way twice.

Essay No. 12

The Lake in Every Season, and the One I Choose

LandscapeWritten October 2023

People who don't know the lake assume it is one thing — blue, or not blue, present, a fixture. It is not. In spring it is a mirror so still that the hills grow a second, upside-down set of themselves in the water, and boys skim stones across both landscapes at once. But I want to write about the lake in the dry months, in May and June, when the water pulls back from its own shoreline and leaves a wide grey collar of cracked mud, salt-crusted, littered with the shells of things that lived there when the water was higher.

This is the lake no one photographs. It looks like failure, like retreat. But walking that collar of dried mud, I have found it is the only time you can see how the lake actually sits in the land — not as a postcard blue disc but as a bowl, a depression, a shape the hills have been holding for longer than any of us have been alive. The dry lake tells the truth the full lake hides.

I think of it sometimes when a system I've built is running clean and green, no errors, nothing visible. I want the dry season version. I want to see the shape underneath.

So when people ask my favorite season, I say the one with the least water, and watch them try to work out whether I'm joking. I am not. A thing you love at its fullest is easy; anyone can love the mirror. The dry collar of mud, the exposed stones, the herons standing where the deep water used to be — that is the lake without its performance on. If you can love it then, exposed and unbeautiful and entirely itself, then the blue months are just a bonus the year sometimes pays.

Essay No. 13

What Grows Where It Shouldn't

LandscapeWritten November 2023

On the wall of the old fort above Kallar Kahar — the one nobody maintains, whose Mughal-era stones are the color of old bone — there is a wild fig tree growing directly out of the mortar, its roots splayed sideways across the stone like fingers spread flat on a table. No one planted it. A bird dropped a seed into a crack decades ago, probably, and the crack held just enough dust and rain for the seed to take.

Now the tree is taller than the wall itself, and its roots have started to work the stones apart, patient and unhurried, the way water works stone. Everyone who sees it says the same thing: it shouldn't be there. And they are right, structurally. But I go back to it more than I go back to almost anywhere else in town, because it is the clearest evidence I know that a place can hold two truths without apologizing for either: the fort is a ruin, and the fort is alive.

I don't think those are in tension. I think the tree is what a ruin looks like when it refuses to finish ruining.

I took a photograph of it once, meaning to show someone, and the picture flattened it into nothing — a smudge of green on grey stone. Some things refuse to be carried away from themselves. So instead I describe it, badly, the way I am describing it now: a tree that was never planted, growing out of a wall that was never meant to hold one, both of them slowly becoming a single thing. The fort is four hundred years into falling down. The fig, as far as I can tell, is just getting started.

Essay No. 14

The Quiet of a Specific Place

LandscapeWritten December 2023

Everyone says the hills are quiet, and everyone is wrong, or at least imprecise. The quiet of the ridge above our house at noon is not the quiet of the same ridge at four in the morning, and neither is the quiet you get standing at the lake's edge just after the last minibus to Chakwal has pulled away. Noon quiet has weight to it — the heat presses sound down, so what you hear is close and small: a single dry leaf, your own blood in your ears.

Four a.m. quiet is enormous and cold, and inside it you can hear a dog three villages away deciding whether to bark. Lake-at-dusk quiet is the strangest, because it isn't silence at all — it's water sound, wind in the reeds, a boatman's oar — but it reads as quiet because none of those sounds are human.

I have tried, more than once, to explain this distinction to people who grew up in cities, and they nod politely and don't believe me. You cannot describe a specific quiet. You can only stand in one long enough to notice it isn't like the others.

The machines I work with know only one quiet: the absence of error output. A silent terminal means nothing to say, and nothing to say means health. It took me years to realize I had learned a whole taxonomy of silence long before I ever opened a console — that the hills had already taught me quiet comes in species, each with its own weight and temperature. Now, in hostel rooms and labs, when someone says "it's quiet," some part of me still asks: which kind? They rarely have an answer. I usually do.

Essay No. 15

A Fixed Point

LandscapeWritten January 2024

There is a single sarr tree — the local name for it, though I've never learned the botanical one — at the crest of the hill behind our old house, and it has been there, unmistakably itself, since before I was born. My father has a photograph of it from his own boyhood, black and white, the tree already old in that picture.

I have watched it from every window I have ever had in that house. I measured my growing against it the way other children measure against a doorframe — not literally, but in the sense that it was always there when I looked up, always the same shape against the sky, while I changed constantly underneath it. When I left for university, it was the sarr tree I pictured, not the house.

Fixed points are strange to love because you cannot love them the way you love a person, with reciprocity, with change on both sides. The tree does not know me. It has simply refused, for decades, to be anywhere else. Maybe that is its own kind of loyalty. Maybe fixed points are what let everything else move.

Last winter I climbed up to it for the first time in years and stood inside its shadow instead of looking at it from below, and the strangest thing happened: the hill rearranged itself. Everything I had ever located by the tree — the house, the road, the water — swung around the moment I stood where it stands. That is the thing about fixed points. You can orient your whole life by one for twenty years, and it will never once acknowledge the arrangement. Then one day you go and stand next to it, and you are the landmark, briefly, and the view belongs to someone else.

Essay No. 16

What the Storm Gave Instead

LandscapeWritten February 2024

We had planned, that August, to walk to the far side of the lake for a wedding function — cousins, aunts, the whole slow procession of people in good clothes not built for hiking. Twenty minutes in, the sky did the thing it does in the Salt Range in late summer: turned the color of a bruise and opened without warning. Everyone scattered for the nearest cover, which turned out to be the veranda of a stranger's house, a small stone structure with a tin roof that made the rain sound like static.

We were stuck there for almost two hours — twelve or thirteen of us, soaked, missing the very event we'd dressed for — while the family whose porch we'd invaded brought out tea, then biscuits, then, eventually, their own stories, because what else do you do with thirteen strangers on your veranda in a downpour.

I don't remember much about the wedding we eventually reached, wet-hemmed and late. I remember the porch. I remember an old woman there telling a story about her husband's first job that made my mother laugh so hard she had to sit down. The plan failed completely. Something else, unplanned and better, filled the two hours the plan would have used.

I think about that porch whenever a plan collapses now — a build failing an hour before a deadline, a bus missed by thirty seconds. The storm took the afternoon we wanted and handed us a different one, and the trade, measured across years, was not even close. Nobody photographs the afternoon that replaced the plan. There is no picture of us on that porch, wet shoes lined at the step, listening to a stranger's story while the rain rewrote the day. It is one of my clearest memories of the lake, and the lake is not even in it.

Essay No. 17

The Last Empty Place

LandscapeWritten February 2024

There used to be a stretch of scrubland between our house and the lake road — nothing on it, not even goats most days, just low thorn bushes and packed reddish earth and, if you were patient, the occasional sighting of a mongoose crossing between rocks. It wasn't beautiful in any way you could photograph. It was simply unclaimed, and I understood even as a child that this was rare and getting rarer.

Last year they began marking it out for a housing scheme — surveyor's stakes with pink ribbon, a bulldozer parked at the edge like a promise. I went and walked it once more before the marking started properly, not because I thought I could stop anything, but because I wanted to have walked it as itself, one more time, before it became a lot number and a foundation.

I don't have a tidy conclusion about development or progress. I know the town needs houses. I also know that I now live in a place with one fewer stretch of ground that belonged to no one in particular, and I notice its absence the way you notice a missing tooth — with your tongue, uselessly, again and again.

What I miss, I've realized, is not the scrubland itself but what it charged for admission: nothing. It asked no purpose of you. You could cross it on the way to somewhere or stand in the middle of it on the way to nowhere, and it made no distinction. The housing scheme will be useful, and the families who live there will love it in their own way, and both of these things can be true alongside mine. But every town has a finite supply of places that ask nothing. We spent one. I hope whoever counts these things is keeping a ledger somewhere.

Essay No. 18

A Landscape Seen Once

LandscapeWritten March 2024

On a school trip in ninth grade we drove north toward Naran, and somewhere past Balakot the bus rounded a curve and the valley opened onto a single mountain, entirely white, that seemed to occupy the whole windshield for perhaps four seconds before the road curved again and trees swallowed it. I have never been back. I don't even know, with certainty, which peak it was.

But I remember the mountain with a clarity I don't have for places I've visited a dozen times. I think this is because it asked nothing of me. I didn't have to plan around it, photograph it correctly, or manage the logistics of being there. It simply appeared, entire, and then it was gone, and my only job was to have seen it.

I wonder sometimes if that is the purest way to encounter a landscape — accidentally, briefly, without the burden of purpose — and whether the reason we build elaborate trips to "see" places is that we no longer trust ourselves to notice anything we haven't paid for.

I have been back to that valley since, or near it — close enough to look for the curve, the bend where the bus turned and the mountain arrived. I didn't find it. Either the road has changed, or I have, or the mountain only performs once per customer. I've made peace with the possibility that the memory is unverifiable, because its unreliability is part of the gift. A landscape seen once belongs to you completely, in a way no lived-in place ever can. Kallar Kahar I share with everyone who has ever stood on its ridge. That mountain, whoever it was, is mine alone.

Essay No. 19

What Only Makes Sense Up Close

LandscapeWritten April 2024

From the ridge, the salt seams in the hills around Kallar Kahar look like nothing much — faint pink-white streaks running through grey-brown rock, the kind of detail your eye slides past. You have to walk right up to a cut face, put your hand on it, to understand what you're looking at: that the pink is not paint or stain but the actual substance of the hill, that these mountains are, in some real sense, made of the same mineral my mother keeps in a jar in the kitchen.

Up close you can see the crystalline structure catching light, tiny facets, an architecture at a scale no distant view could ever suggest. I think about this a great deal in the context of the systems I study, which behave the same way — clean and smooth from a distance, a black box with inputs and outputs, and then, the moment you actually open the code, revealed as thousands of small deliberate decisions.

Distance flatters everything into simplicity. Only proximity tells you what a thing is actually made of.

Engineering school, it turns out, is largely the formal study of this principle. A circuit diagram is a distant view — clean lines, ideal components, everything legible. Then you build the thing and lean in close and discover the solder joint with its tiny crystalline fractures, the resistor running slightly warm, the actual grainy texture of a system that exists in the world. I have learned to distrust any understanding I haven't stood next to. The ridge view is where you decide what deserves a closer look. It is never, by itself, the truth.

Essay No. 20

Photograph Versus Presence

LandscapeWritten May 2024

There is a photograph of the lake at sunset that half of Kallar Kahar has taken, more or less identically, from the same viewpoint near the parking area — the water gone copper, the hills silhouetted, a boat if you're lucky. I have taken it myself, more than once, and it is a good photograph. It is also, I've come to believe, almost nothing like being there.

What the photograph cannot hold is the smell of the reeds warming all day and releasing it now, at dusk, in a slow green exhale. It cannot hold the specific cold that comes off water at that hour, or the sound of the last fisherman's oar, or the fact that your feet are tired and your family is calling you to come eat.

The photograph preserves the one sense a camera has access to and discards the four it doesn't, and somehow we have all agreed to call the resulting image "the view," as though sight were the whole of a place. It isn't. It's the postcard we send our own memory, and memory, being lazier than we'd like, often accepts it.

I still take the photograph. Everyone does; the light at that hour practically insists. But I've stopped confusing the image with the evening, the way I've stopped confusing a transcript with a lecture or a schema with a database full of actual rows. The picture is a receipt — proof of attendance, nothing more. The evening itself happened to all of me at once, and the portion that fit through a lens is the portion I trust least, precisely because it can be carried away and shown to people who weren't there, wearing the authority of the whole.

Essay No. 21

Belonging to No One and Everyone

FamilyWritten June 2024

In the sitting room of our house there is a brass tray, dented slightly on one side, that has never belonged to any single person's story. It isn't my mother's dowry piece — that one lives in her almirah, wrapped in cloth. It isn't a wedding gift with a name attached. It simply appeared, at some point before my own memory starts, and has been used every single day since.

No one has ever told its story because, I suspect, no one entirely remembers it. It belongs to the house the way the walls belong to the house. I think every family has one or two objects like this — orphaned of provenance, adopted by sheer daily use — and that they are, in their unglamorous way, more central to a household than the objects everyone can narrate.

The named things get preserved, wrapped, protected from use. The unnamed things get worn down by exactly the kind of use that makes a house a house.

I used it last, I think, to carry cups of chai out to the veranda when my aunt visited in the spring — four cups, a sugar pot, the tray doing its uncelebrated arithmetic of balance on my forearm. Somewhere in a lab I use there is a server that has run, uninterrupted, for longer than some of my classmates have been alive, and no one has ever told its story either. The tray and the server are the same kind of object: load-bearing, unphotographed, essential. The named things in a house get the shelf. The unnamed things get the work.

Essay No. 22

A Skill Absorbed, Never Taught

FamilyWritten July 2024

My mother can tell, from the sound alone, whether the daal on the stove needs another five minutes or is about to catch and burn — not by smell, not by looking, just by the particular pitch the bubbling makes as it thickens. I have never once seen her explain this to anyone, including me. When I asked her how she knows, she looked at me as though I'd asked how she knows it's daytime.

She doesn't know how she knows. It was never a lesson; it accumulated, the way a language accumulates in a child who is never formally taught grammar and simply absorbs the shape of correct sentences by being spoken to for years.

I have spent four years in classrooms being taught things explicitly, with slides and structure and stated learning outcomes, and I sometimes envy the other kind of knowledge — the kind you cannot trace to a lecture, that arrived through nothing but proximity and repetition. I don't have my mother's ear for daal. I have a different, stated, credentialed kind of knowing. I am not sure it runs as deep.

I tried to learn it formally once — stood at the stove with a timer and a notebook, determined to convert her listening into procedure. The daal burned while I wrote things down. There is a lesson in that I've never quite gotten over: some knowledge exists only at the speed of attention, and the moment you slow it down enough to transcribe, you've already changed what it is. She laughs when I tell her this. "It's just daal," she says. But I have watched her do it a hundred times now, and I am telling you: it is not just daal. It is a whole epistemology, simmering.

Essay No. 23

The Rule No One Questioned

FamilyWritten July 2024

No one in our house ever raised their voice at the dinner table — not in anger, not in excitement, not even in the exuberant retelling of good news. It was never announced as a rule. It simply was the temperature of the room, established so early and so consistently that by the time I was old enough to notice other families operated differently, I found it almost disorienting.

I used to think this quietness was a kind of repression, and maybe in some households it would be. In ours, I've come to understand it differently: as a discipline my father brought home from decades of postings where composure under pressure wasn't a personality trait but a professional requirement, absorbed so completely it became simply how a table should sound.

I don't know if I'll raise my own children the same way. I know that when I am now in loud rooms, some part of me still flinches, waiting for the volume to mean something has gone wrong.

What I understand now that I didn't then is that the rule was never about silence. It was about the table — about keeping one place in the day where nothing could be won. Everywhere else, voices rose: in the courtyard, over the phone, at the gate. But dinner was Switzerland, and we were all, without ever agreeing to it, citizens. I notice myself defending the same border now in other rooms — closing my laptop when the food arrives, letting an argument cool on the stove of an unfinished sentence. The rule no one questioned turned out to be load-bearing. Most of them are.

Essay No. 24

The Habit I Swore I'd Never Pick Up

FamilyWritten August 2024

My father checks every lock in the house before bed — not once, the way anyone might, but in a specific sequence, front door, then the gate, then back to the front door a second time, as though the first check might have been a dream. I am, as of this year, someone who runs the same unit test twice before deploying anything, who reads a submitted assignment one extra time after I've already decided it's finished, who has, more than once, walked back to a locked door I already knew was locked.

I used to think I'd inherited his caution as a flaw, a nervous tic passed down without my consent. Lately I think it might be the opposite — that vigilance, when it comes from someone who spent a career responsible for things that could not afford to fail, is not anxiety so much as respect for consequence.

The engineers I study with would call this defense in depth, and they'd mean it as a compliment. Somewhere between his gate latch and my second test run, the family trade passed down without either of us signing for it. He checks the locks because the world contains uncertainty; I rerun the tests for exactly the same reason, in a smaller, more obedient world. I still tease him about the sequence. He still does it every night. And I have stopped swearing I'll never pick things up, because it turns out the habits we mock are just the ones we haven't needed yet.

Essay No. 25

The Meal for One Occasion

FamilyWritten September 2024

No one else in the extended family marks this date.
