Now that I know the story, the dish reads entirely differently to me: not a recipe but an act of memory performed annually. Some meals feed you. This one feeds a memory instead, and we are simply the ones who get to eat what's left over.

I've asked her for the recipe twice. Both times she's given it to me slightly wrong — I am certain of this now, though it took years to suspect — not out of secrecy but because the actual recipe includes the day itself, and that can't be dictated. Some dishes are food. This one is a calendar, a memorial, and an argument about what deserves remembering, all layered under saffron. When I make it myself someday, on some future version of that date, it will taste different in my kitchen. I think that's the point. The dish was never meant to be preserved. It was meant to be re-performed.

Essay No. 26

What Everyone Knows and No One Says

FamilyWritten October 2024

There is a framed photograph on the shelf in the hallway of a cousin who does not visit anymore, and no one has ever sat me down to explain why. I know, in the way you know weather patterns without reading a forecast, that something happened between him and my father's side of the family, a rift severe enough to end visits but not severe enough to remove the photograph.

Every family I've ever been inside a room with has at least one version of this — a name that produces a particular silence, a subject the conversation steps around the way you step around a crack in the pavement, automatically, without looking down.

I used to find this frustrating, as though the family were withholding a story that was rightfully mine. I've come to think of it differently now: some silences are not secrets so much as unfinished griefs, still too live to be handled in words, kept instead in the shape of an absence everyone has quietly agreed to respect.

The photograph stays on the shelf, face out, which is its own kind of sentence — not removed, not discussed, simply kept in the grammar of the hallway where everyone can see it and no one conjugates it. I used to think understanding a family meant eventually learning all its stories. Now I think it means learning the shape of its silences and not pressing on them. Whatever happened, it produced a silence that has outlasted every explanation anyone could have given me. I have learned to walk past it the way everyone else does: slowly enough to acknowledge it, quickly enough to leave it intact.

Essay No. 27

The Sound That Means Someone Specific

FamilyWritten November 2024

My father's motorcycle — an old thing he refuses to replace — makes a distinct cough-and-catch sound when it starts up in the lane outside our gate, different from every other engine on our street, and I have known that sound since before I could name it. I used to hear it from my room and know, with total certainty, that he was home, still an hour before I'd see him.

My mother has a version of this too: the particular double-knock she uses on my door, unlike anyone else's knock, that meant food was ready or a call had come for me. These sounds are not language. They carry no content you could write down.

And yet I would know either of them anywhere, in any country, decades from now — they are among the most permanently encoded things I possess. I think a family is partly built out of exactly this: a private acoustic vocabulary, unteachable to outsiders, that tells you who has arrived before you've looked up.

Technology keeps promising to replace this with better signals — ringtones assigned per contact, notifications with names attached, every sound labeled and sorted. But the labeled sounds carry less than the recognized ones. A ringtone tells you who is calling; my father's motorcycle told you he was home, which is a different fact entirely, and a warmer one. I think about this when I design systems now, when I choose what a notification should say. Information is cheap. Recognition — the kind built over ten thousand repetitions, the kind you couldn't transfer to anyone else if you tried — that is the expensive thing.

Essay No. 28

How Affection Actually Gets Shown

FamilyWritten December 2024

On television, affection has a grammar I recognize but did not grow up speaking — the declared "I love you," the embrace held for the camera. In my house, affection has always looked more like this: my father peeling an orange completely, every pith removed, before handing me the segments. My mother re-folding a shirt I'd already folded badly, not as criticism but as care disguised as correction.

For a long time I measured my family against the television version and came up short, wondering if we were somehow less demonstrative than we should be. I don't think that anymore. I think every family develops its own private dialect of care, and that dialect is often untranslatable into the more universal, more filmable language of hugs and stated declarations.

My family's dialect is logistical. It shows up as an orange with no pith, a shirt folded twice, a question about food. I have learned to hear "I love you" inside all three, even though none of them contain the words.

I have started, quietly, to answer in the same dialect. I peel the orange now. I fold the shirt. I ask whether she's eaten before I say anything else, and I hear myself doing it, and I don't correct course. Every family has a language like this underneath the one it speaks — a set of small logistical gestures that carry the entire emotional payload of the household. Ours just happens to run on fruit and folded cotton and questions about food. It took me twenty years to learn I was fluent. I had been speaking it, without an accent, the whole time.

Essay No. 29

A Disagreement Understood Differently Now

FamilyWritten December 2024

When I chose computer engineering over the medical track my father had quietly hoped for, there was a stretch of some months where our conversations became careful in a way they'd never been before — polite, slightly formal, both of us avoiding the actual subject. I remember being furious at the time, certain he simply didn't understand what the field meant or could become.

I understand it differently now, with four years and a great deal more context behind me. He grew up in a generation and a profession where security was not a preference but a survival strategy, where a stable, legible path mattered more than passion because the alternative had real costs he had personally watched people pay. He wasn't rejecting my interest. He was translating risk through the only lens available to him.

We never had the conversation where either of us said this explicitly — some disagreements in families resolve not through discussion but through time simply proving one side's fears wrong or right. Mine seem, so far, to be proving him wrong about the risk and right, in his own way, about something else: that he only ever wanted me somewhere solid.

He came to my last project demonstration, stood in a lab full of hardware he couldn't name, and watched me explain a system to a room of evaluators. On the drive home he said almost nothing about it, which in our family's dialect is a speech. I have stopped needing the explicit conversation. The disagreement didn't get resolved; it got absorbed, the way a river absorbs a tributary — the water doesn't argue about direction, it just becomes one thing going somewhere. He wanted safety for me. I found it in a place he couldn't have pointed to on a map. Both of us were right. The river knows.

Essay No. 30

What I Inherited That Isn't a Thing

FamilyWritten January 2025

I did not inherit money from my grandmother, or property, or jewelry — what came down to me instead, I've realized only in retrospect, was a specific way of finishing what you start even after the reason for starting it has stopped mattering. She raised five children largely alone during years my family doesn't discuss in detail, and everyone who remembers her says the same thing: she did not quit tasks halfway, regardless of circumstance.

That trait skipped a generation in visible form and landed, somehow, in me — I am the one in the family who cannot leave a half-finished assignment, half-read book, half-fixed piece of code alone overnight. My mother says I have her mother's hands for it, though I never met her.

I think inheritance is usually imagined as objects, as things you can hold and appraise, but the realest inheritances might be exactly this — a disposition, a way of meeting difficulty, passed down with no ceremony and no paperwork, discovered only when you notice yourself doing something an ancestor did, for reasons you've never been told.

I keep a photograph of her above my desk now, and some evenings, stuck on a problem that won't yield, I catch myself doing the thing — the jaw set, the refusal to stand up, the quiet insistence that the work will finish because leaving it is not among the available options. It is the strangest heirloom: no appraiser would value it, no sibling could contest it, and I use it every single day. Money gets spent and property gets sold, but a disposition compounds. Whatever she was building with all that stubbornness across all those years, some portion of it is still under construction. The site has just moved.

Essay No. 31

The First Almost-Human Moment

TechnologyWritten February 2025

I remember the first time a piece of code I had written responded to an edge case I hadn't anticipated and handled it correctly anyway — not because I'd foreseen that exact input, but because the logic I'd built was, without my fully realizing it, general enough to cover a case I'd never imagined. It was a small university assignment, nothing remarkable by any technical standard.

But there was a strange half-second where the machine seemed to know something I hadn't told it, and I felt a genuine, almost superstitious jolt, the sense of having built something slightly larger than my own understanding of it. I've since learned exactly why this happens — generalization, abstraction, the mathematics of it are not mysterious at all.

But that first jolt has never fully left me. I think it's the moment most engineers privately remember as the reason they kept going: the instant a system you built stopped feeling like a list of instructions and started feeling, briefly and falsely but vividly, like it understood something.

I've told this story to non-engineers and watched it die in the telling, because from the outside it sounds like what it technically was: a conditional executing correctly. You have to have been alone with a system at 2 a.m., certain of its limits, and then watched it exceed them, to understand why I sat back in my chair like the room had shifted. The machine didn't know anything, of course. The knowledge was mine, deposited earlier and forgotten, and the code was just returning it to me with interest. But for one half-second, the boundary between built and born flickered. I've been chasing that flicker ever since.

Essay No. 32

The Skill I'm Losing to a Device

TechnologyWritten March 2025

I used to be able to navigate the roads between Kallar Kahar and Chakwal entirely from memory — every turn, every landmark, built up over years of being driven and, later, driving. I noticed last year that I no longer trust that memory the way I used to; I check my phone even for routes I could probably still recite correctly, because the checking has become reflexive.

This bothers me more than it probably should, because I recognize the exact same erosion happening with mental arithmetic, with spelling, with the small daily calculations I used to do in my head and now outsource by default.

I don't think the tools are wrong to exist. I think what unsettles me is how quietly the trade happens — no single decision to stop remembering routes, just years of a faster option sitting one tap away, until one day you notice the old skill has gone soft, like a language you used to speak fluently and now have to reach for.

So last month, driving home, I turned the navigation off at the Motorway exit and did the rest from memory — badly, with two wrong turns and one stop to ask a man outside a shop who gave directions entirely in landmarks, the way directions used to be given. It took twenty minutes longer. It was worth it. Somewhere between the wrong turns I felt the old map in my head redraw itself, faint but legible, like a muscle reporting back after years of rest. The phone stayed in my pocket the whole way. The lake, when it appeared, looked exactly like a thing you found yourself.

Essay No. 33

Supposed To Versus Actually Does

TechnologyWritten April 2025

The documentation for the wireless module we used in a systems lab last year described a clean, predictable behavior — connect, transmit, disconnect, repeat, all within stated timing tolerances. What it actually did, under the specific conditions of our lab's aging hardware and slightly too-long cable runs, was drop connections at what appeared to be random intervals.

This gap — between the clean behavior promised on paper and the messy behavior a system actually exhibits once it meets the real world's specific imperfections — is, I've come to believe, the truest subject of engineering, more than any of the theory we're formally taught.

I think about this gap outside of engineering too now — how a rule "supposed to" apply to everyone behaves quite differently once it meets a specific family, a specific town, a specific set of exceptions nobody wrote down. Documentation is a description of intention. Behavior is what happens when intention meets friction.

The world, I have learned, is a lab full of wireless modules. Every institution, every custom, every rule arrives with documentation describing clean and predictable behavior, and every one of them meets the specific impedance of an actual place — this village, this family, this syllabus, this road — and does something slightly off-spec. The engineers who thrive aren't the ones who trust the datasheet or the ones who discard it; they're the ones who measure the gap. I try to do the same with people now: read the documentation, then watch the behavior, and keep my expectations tuned to the difference.

Essay No. 34

Connected Across Distance

TechnologyWritten May 2025

When my cousin moved to Riyadh for work, the calls home were expensive and rare enough that they became formal events — everyone gathered, taking turns, the connection sometimes cutting out mid-sentence. Now she is reachable at almost any hour, in low resolution but real time, and I've watched my aunt's relationship with her daughter's absence change shape entirely as a result.

I don't think this is a simple story about technology solving distance. I think it's a story about technology changing what distance means without removing it. My aunt can see her daughter's face on a screen nightly if she chooses.

She still cannot fix her daughter's tea, or sit beside her in a room, or notice without being told that something is wrong in her voice. The connection is real. It is also, I've come to believe, a different thing entirely from presence, wearing presence's clothes.

What the video call gave us, I eventually understood, was not closeness but schedule — the relief of a standing appointment where absence used to be. And perhaps that is the honest measure of what technology does to distance: it doesn't delete it, it organizes it, gives it a time slot and a mute button. My aunt still lives seven hours of airplane away. But Sunday at 4 p.m. now exists as a place, a small rented room that exists in two countries at once, and on the good calls, when the connection holds and the tea is hot on both ends, the distance sits quietly in the corner and lets the room be a room.

Essay No. 35

What Breaking Taught Me

TechnologyWritten May 2025

A hard drive failure in my second year of university took eleven months of coursework, photos, and half-finished projects with it, all at once, with no warning, on an ordinary Tuesday. At the time it felt like a catastrophe disproportionate to its actual cause — a single component, worth perhaps a few thousand rupees, failing silently.

What it taught me, in the months of reconstruction that followed, was something no functioning system had ever taught me: that redundancy is not paranoia, that a backup is not an insult to your own carefulness but an acknowledgment that carefulness is not sufficient protection against the physical world.

I now back up everything, reflexively, in a way that would have looked excessive to my former self. Most of the lessons I actually carry forward from four years of engineering came not from the systems that worked as intended, but from the handful that failed spectacularly.

The strange thing is that I'm grateful for it now — not in the polished, everything-happens-for-a-reason way, but in the specific way you can only be grateful for a loss you've fully itemized. I know exactly what those eleven months contained, because I rebuilt them file by file. Some things came back improved; some came back as approximations; some didn't come back at all, and I learned which category most of my work falls into. Every system I design now begins with the same question the failure taught me: what happens here on an ordinary Tuesday, with no warning? It is not a cheerful question. It is the most useful one I own.

Essay No. 36

The Last Time There Was No Signal

TechnologyWritten June 2025

There's a stretch of the old road climbing out past the lake, before it drops toward the plains, where the signal simply gives out — no bars, no notification, nothing — for perhaps twenty minutes of driving. I remember the first time I noticed it, years ago, feeling a small flicker of anxiety, as though something had gone wrong with the phone rather than with the geography.

Now I look forward to that stretch specifically. It is one of a shrinking number of places where the decision to check something is made for you, externally, by physics rather than willpower, and there is a peculiar relief in that removal of choice. You look out the window instead. You notice the ridge line, actually notice it.

I've started to wonder whether the appeal of these dead zones isn't really about the absence of connectivity at all, but about the absence of the small, constant decision not to check — a decision that, made a hundred times a day everywhere else, is quietly exhausting in a way we've mostly stopped noticing.

I've started building small dead zones into my ordinary days on purpose — a walk without the phone, an hour with the laptop shut — and they fail constantly, because a manufactured dead zone is a contradiction: the exit is always in your pocket. That is what makes the road past the lake precious. Its deadness is not a feature someone added; it is a fact of geography, older than the network and indifferent to it. You cannot opt back in from the far side of that hill. And until the coverage maps finally close over it — and they will — that stretch of road remains the last place where my attention is not a resource anyone is bidding for.

Essay No. 37

A Tool That Would Baffle 1976

TechnologyWritten July 2025

I spend a fair amount of my coursework now inside version control systems, watching branches of code merge and diverge and merge again, resolving conflicts between two people's simultaneous changes to the exact same file with what has become, to me, an entirely unremarkable piece of software.

I tried explaining this once to my father, describing what it actually does — that two people, working independently, without speaking to each other, can edit the same document and have the changes reconciled automatically — and watched him struggle to picture it, not because he isn't capable, but because the entire category of problem it solves didn't meaningfully exist for most of his working life.

What strikes me most isn't the tool itself but how invisible its strangeness has become to me. I think every generation's engineers carry, unnoticed, a set of tools that would have counted as something close to magic to the generation before them, and that the marker of true fluency is exactly this: the magic has worn off and become mere infrastructure.

I keep a small private museum of these moments now: the tool that would bewitch my grandfather, the workflow that would scandalize my father, the abstraction I already can't imagine working without. It has made me gentler about the future, I think. Somewhere there is a student, not yet born, who will learn systems that make my version control look like two tin cans and a string, and she will try to explain them to me, and I will struggle to picture the category of problem they solve. I hope I remember, in that moment, my father's face across the dinner table — and nod, and believe her anyway.

Essay No. 38

Help Versus Replace

TechnologyWritten August 2025

The compiler that catches my syntax errors before I've finished typing a line is, unambiguously, help — it does something I could not efficiently do myself, at a speed that makes the work better, and I have never once felt diminished by leaning on it. Increasingly, though, I use tools that draft entire functions from a description of what I want, and there the line gets harder to locate.

I don't have a settled answer, and I'm suspicious of anyone who claims to. What I've noticed is that the discomfort seems to track not with how much a tool does, but with how much of the understanding it lets me skip.

A spell-checker doesn't threaten my grasp of language, but a tool that reasons through a problem I never had to reason through myself leaves a gap where a skill used to be forming. Help augments a capability you still have to build. Replacement lets the capability quietly go unbuilt.

So I've started keeping a rough ledger, the way my grandmother kept account of household expenses — a mental note, each week, of which thinking I did and which was done for me. Not to purge the tools; I am not interested in purity, and the compiler stays. But the ledger keeps the exchange rate visible. Every convenience costs a small quantity of ability, and most weeks the trade is worth it, and some weeks it isn't, and the only unforgivable option is not knowing which. Help is a gift. Replacement is a transaction. The whole skill of being a person among machines is telling the two apart before you sign.

Essay No. 39

A Technical Rite of Passage

TechnologyWritten September 2025

The first time I got a distributed system of my own design to actually hold consistent state across multiple machines — nothing sophisticated, a class project, three virtual nodes agreeing on a single shared value despite deliberately simulated failures — I stayed up until nearly four in the morning to watch it succeed on the tenth or eleventh attempt, and something in how I understood my own competence shifted permanently that night.

It wasn't the hardest thing I've built since. But it was the first time an abstract concept from a textbook — consensus, fault tolerance, the whole theoretical apparatus — became something I had made behave correctly with my own hands, at four in the morning, alone, with no one to hand the problem to.

I think every field has a moment like this, not officially marked by any ceremony, where a student privately crosses from following instructions to actually understanding the thing the instructions were pointing at. Mine happened at a kitchen table, on a laptop balanced on a stack of books.

No one tells you, when you start a degree, that the qualification is a scaffolding around the real credential, which is this: one unglamorous night, alone, a system of your own making did the thing the textbook said was possible, and you were the reason. Everything since has been elaboration. The nodes were virtual, the value they agreed on was meaningless, the failures were simulated — and none of that matters at all. For one long minute at four in the morning, consensus held because I had understood something correctly, and I sat in the blue light of the terminal feeling the floor of my own capability settle, permanently, one storey lower and firmer than before.

Essay No. 40

What a Piece of Hardware Wants

TechnologyWritten October 2025

The lab's oldest server rack has a personality, and everyone who has worked with it agrees on this, even though none of us would defend the claim philosophically. It wants to be restarted in a specific order — network switch first, then the primary node, a full ninety seconds later the secondaries — and if you deviate from that order, it sulks, refusing connections for reasons no log file ever fully explains.

We have learned its preferences the way you learn a difficult relative's preferences: not through documentation, which is sparse and partly wrong, but through years of accumulated, half-superstitious observation passed down from one cohort of students to the next.

I know this isn't really personality. But I've started to think the impulse to describe a machine's logic as a personality isn't naive so much as efficient — it's a compressed way of encoding "behavior we've observed but can't fully explain," which is, when I'm honest, most of what I actually know about most of the systems I work with.

What the rack actually taught me — what I didn't expect from a systems course — is that all expertise eventually becomes folklore. Documentation decays, vendors vanish, and what remains is the maintained, corrected, lovingly inaccurate body of knowledge passed between the people who touch the machine. Every craft has this. My mother has it with her stove, which runs hot on the left. The rack has it with its moods. We are not wrong to speak of these things as personalities; we are just compressing a thousand observations into a single usable fiction. It is the oldest engineering trick there is. We learned it around fires, long before there were servers.

Essay No. 41

A Smell That Returns One Year

MemoryWritten October 2025

The smell of rain hitting hot, dry earth — petrichor, the word I only learned later, in a chemistry class that felt almost insulting for naming something so private — takes me back specifically to the summer I was nine, to a single afternoon whose actual events I can no longer reconstruct in any detail.

I don't remember what happened that day. I remember only the smell, and the particular quality of light just before a storm, gold going grey, and a feeling of enormous, wordless anticipation that I have never since attached to any other memory as cleanly.

Every year, at the first real rain after the dry season, that same afternoon returns for a few seconds, entirely intact and entirely useless — a memory with all its emotional weight preserved and almost none of its content. Nothing else I own returns so completely, or explains so little about what it's returning me to.

What I've never told anyone is that I've started to look forward to the theft — the three or four seconds each year when the smell takes the afternoon back and I am eleven again, standing in a doorway I no longer have access to, watching rain arrive like a guest the whole town had been waiting for. It is the closest thing I own to time travel, and it costs nothing, and it cannot be improved or scheduled or saved. Chemistry gave it a name and, in doing so, nearly made it ordinary. But the first rain after the dry season doesn't care what we call it. It just opens the door.

Essay No. 42

A Memory My Family Doesn't Share

MemoryWritten November 2025

There is a version of the day we moved from my father's last posting back to Kallar Kahar for good that exists only in my own memory, unconfirmed by anyone else present. I remember it as golden, almost ceremonial. When I've mentioned this to my mother, she remembers the same day as exhausting and logistically miserable, dominated by a fight with the moving company.

Neither of us is lying. We were, apparently, standing in the same driveway experiencing entirely different days. I used to find this troubling, as though it meant memory couldn't be trusted at all.

I've come to think of it differently now — that a single event doesn't produce one memory to be shared but as many memories as there were people old enough to form one, each shaped by what that particular person needed the day to mean. My mother needed it to end. I needed it to matter. We were both right.

This used to feel like a defect in the family — as though the group memory had a bug, a record that failed to sync. Now I think the divergence is the point. A family is not a database that must agree with itself; it is more like the systems I study, where each node keeps its own copy and perfect consistency is not just impossible but unnecessary. My version of that driveway belongs to me alone now, unverifiable and therefore unchangeable, and somewhere my mother keeps hers, and the day itself — whatever it objectively was — belongs to no one at all. We each got a copy. We each got to keep it.

Essay No. 43

The Last Ordinary Day

MemoryWritten December 2025

I can't identify, with any precision, the last completely ordinary day before my father's final posting was announced and everything in the following two years reorganized around the eventual return home — which is, I think, the actual nature of such days. They never announce themselves.

Somewhere in that stretch there was a Tuesday, unremarkable, that was in fact the last one of its kind, and I walked through it without noticing, the way you walk past a landmark for the final time without knowing it's the final time.

I've become slightly obsessed, since realizing this, with paying closer attention to ordinary days now, on the theory that some current one is quietly the last of its kind too. I don't think the attention actually preserves anything. But it feels, at least, like less of a betrayal of the days that already passed unnoticed.

I can't recover that Tuesday, obviously. It is spent, down to the hour. But the obsession it left behind has turned out to be a gift disguised as a regret: I keep small records now, deliberately boring ones — what the light did this afternoon, what was said at breakfast, the exact arrangement of an unremarkable evening. Most of it will never matter. That is precisely the point. The last ordinary day never announces itself at the door. It walks in dressed as every other day, and the only respectful response is to take attendance, daily, of a life that feels permanent and is not.

Essay No. 44

A Place I Won't Return To

MemoryWritten January 2026

My grandfather's house in a village not far from Kallar Kahar was sold not long after his death, and I have not been back since, nor do I expect to. I remember the house in fragments rather than as a whole: a specific creak in the third step of the staircase, a courtyard tree whose fruit I was told, probably falsely, was poisonous, a particular cool darkness in the store room where the grain was kept.

I have no photographs of most of these details — they were never the kind of thing anyone thought to photograph, being too ordinary, too permanent-seeming to require documentation. Now they exist only where they've always existed, in memory, with no external anchor to correct or confirm them.

I think this is the real cost of a place you'll never revisit — not the loss of the place itself, but the loss of the ability to check your memory of it against anything real.

There is a corner of my mind where the house still stands exactly as it was, and I have learned not to trust it entirely — memory renovates without permission, repaints, moves doors. But I keep the rooms anyway, unverifiable as they are, because the alternative is letting the sale finalize completely. Somewhere in the Salt Range the courtyard is someone else's now; perhaps another child cracks walnuts on that threshold, not knowing it is a museum of anyone's childhood. I hope the house is kind to them. It holds, after all, two histories now — theirs, which is real, and mine, which is the only version I will ever be able to visit.

Essay No. 45

What I Was Wrong About

MemoryWritten February 2026

Until I was perhaps eleven, I believed with total conviction that the lake had no bottom — that it simply continued down indefinitely, connected somehow to something vast and unmapped beneath the hills. An older cousin had told me this, half as a joke, and I had received it as fact, and it had genuinely shaped how I felt about swimming there.

Learning the actual depth, years later — unremarkable, measurable, entirely known — felt like a small private demotion, as though the lake itself had gotten smaller the moment it became knowable.

I think most of childhood's wrongness works this way: not as embarrassing error to be corrected and forgotten, but as a genuine loss of scale, a shrinking of the world's mystery down to its actual, more modest dimensions. I don't wish I still believed it. But I remember exactly what it felt like to believe it, and I think that feeling is worth remembering accurately, even after the belief itself is gone.

I keep a small collection of these demotions now, the way other people keep trophies: the bottomless lake, bottomed; the mountain that turned out to be climbable; the adult certainties that dissolved on inspection. Each one shrank the world and, somehow, made it more habitable — because a world with edges is a world you can actually walk. The infinite is not a gift to a child; it is just the child's name for the unmeasured. I lost a bottomless lake and gained a real one, ninety feet at its deepest, warm in summer, cold in winter, entirely finite, entirely sufficient. It turns out the measurable can still be magnificent. It just has to work harder.

Essay No. 46

The Photograph I Don't Have

MemoryWritten March 2026

No one photographed my mother teaching me to read, which happened, as far as I can reconstruct it, on the covered part of our old veranda, over what must have been months, using a set of Urdu primers with cracked spines that I don't think anyone kept either. I have photographs of far less significant afternoons simply because someone happened to have a camera in hand at the right moment.

The actual formation of my ability to read, arguably one of the more consequential things that has ever happened to me, exists in no image at all, preserved only as a general, undated impression of my mother's finger moving under a line of text and her voice repeating a word until I got it.

I think about this asymmetry often — how thoroughly documented our celebrations are, and how undocumented our actual becoming tends to be. The photographs we have flatter the wrong events. The ones we're missing would have shown us something truer.

So I have started, in a small and private way, correcting the record. I do not photograph the ceremonies anymore — everyone does that. I write down, instead, the undocumented things: the sound of my mother reading a recipe aloud, the exact slowness of my father teaching me to check the oil in a generator, the afternoon a concept finally made sense. None of it will trend. All of it is the actual archive of how a person gets made. The camera pointed at the cake; the becoming happened off to the side, unlit, unrecorded. I am trying to be the photographer who turns, at last, toward the unlit part of the room.

Essay No. 47

Who I've Become

MemoryWritten March 2026

I found an old notebook from when I was perhaps thirteen, filled with plans for what I then called my "future life" — a list that included becoming a doctor, living permanently in Kallar Kahar, and never, under any circumstances, learning to code, which thirteen-year-old me had apparently decided was boring in a way she felt strongly enough to write down.

I am, four years into a computer engineering degree, someone that girl would not recognize and might not entirely approve of. This used to unsettle me slightly, reading it — a sense of having betrayed some earlier, purer version of my own intentions.

I don't feel that anymore. I think thirteen-year-old me was operating with the information she had, and the actual arc of becoming someone is not a betrayal of your earlier selves but a series of honest updates. I try to extend the same patience toward whoever I'll have become by thirty, reading this.

I keep the notebook anyway — not as a map, since I followed almost none of it, but as a record of the weather that particular thirteen-year-old was standing in. She could only want what she could see from where she stood: the lake in front of her, the town around it, the few professions visible from the ridge. I live now in a country she couldn't have imagined, full of compilers and consensus protocols and four-in-the-morning breakthroughs, and I am, in ways she'd find bewildering, happy. Becoming someone is not the betrayal of the girl with the list. It is the repayment. She supplied the wanting. I supplied the information. We are even.

Essay No. 48

A Goodbye That Didn't Feel Like One

MemoryWritten April 2026

The last ordinary conversation I had with my grandmother, weeks before she died unexpectedly, was about nothing in particular — whether I'd eaten, whether the roads were bad, a mild complaint about a neighbor's chickens getting into her garden again. I remember being slightly impatient to get off the phone, mid-exam-season, distracted.

Had I known it was the last one, I obviously would have stayed on the line, said something more deliberate. But that is precisely what a real goodbye almost never announces itself as. It arrives disguised as an ordinary Tuesday conversation about chickens, and you only learn, retroactively, which conversations were actually load-bearing.

I think this is part of why the loss carried a particular kind of guilt beyond the grief itself — not guilt over anything I did wrong, but guilt over the ordinariness, as though the conversation should have known to be more important than it felt at the time.

What I do now, because of that phone call, is unremarkable and slightly absurd: I end ordinary conversations well. I say the small affectionate thing at the end of calls home, not because I expect catastrophe, but because I have learned that every goodbye in a long relationship is dressed as an ordinary moment, and you are never told which costume is final. It costs nothing — a sentence, a second of deliberateness — and it pays out in the only currency grief accepts. She would find the habit funny, I think, and a little sentimental. She'd be right. It is the most useful thing she ever taught me, and she taught it entirely by accident.

Essay No. 49

What a Stranger Did

MemoryWritten May 2026

On a bus from Rawalpindi, years ago, I was traveling alone for the first time, visibly nervous about it in whatever small ways a person betrays nervousness, and an older woman I never learned the name of simply moved seats without comment to sit beside me for the remainder of the journey, saying almost nothing, occasionally pointing out a landmark as though we were old acquaintances.

She got off two stops before mine and I never saw her again. I don't know if she noticed my nervousness and decided to help, or if she simply preferred that seat, and the comfort I felt was incidental to her actual reasoning. It doesn't matter.

I think about her more than I think about people I've known for years, because she asked for nothing and offered a specific, correctly-calibrated kind of company at a moment I genuinely needed it, then disappeared without ever making it about herself. I'm not sure it's a skill you can practice into. I think it might just be a kind of attention some people carry naturally, and I got lucky enough to sit next to it once.

I have tried, since, to be that person in smaller rooms — to notice the visible nervousness of someone doing a thing for the first time, and to offer exactly one calibrated kindness: not rescue, not attention, just a small structural fact delivered at the right moment. It is a harder skill than it sounds. It requires watching strangers closely enough to see what they need and respectfully enough not to need them to see you. I never learned her name, and the bus route has probably changed by now. But somewhere in my personal engineering there is a load-bearing kindness installed by a woman who got off two stops early and never knew what she built.

Essay No. 50

The Story Told Differently

MemoryWritten June 2026

In my family's retelling, the story of how my parents met has calcified into something almost formal — a proposal through relatives, a brief meeting, a decision made with appropriate speed and appropriate caution, everyone behaving exactly as they should have. I believe this version is broadly true.

I also suspect, from a few things my mother has let slip in less guarded moments, that it omits a specific afternoon of genuine uncertainty on her part, a real hesitation she has since folded quietly out of the official account because it doesn't serve the tidy narrative a family likes to keep of itself.

I would tell it differently if it were mine to tell — I would keep the hesitation in, because I think a story that admits its subject once wasn't sure is a truer story than one where everyone always already knew. But it isn't mine to tell. Every family keeps an official version and at least one shadow version, and the shadow version usually belongs to whoever was most uncertain at the time.

I don't think I'll ever actually tell it differently out loud — some stories belong to the family the way a river belongs to its banks, and you don't reroute them on a whim. But knowing the fuller version has changed how I read every other story we tell. Behind each polished one, I now assume, there is a rougher draft: an afternoon of uncertainty, a door almost not opened, a person briefly free to have chosen otherwise. The polished versions are beautiful. The drafts are true. And maybe the most loving thing you can do with a family's mythology is hold both at once — the story as told, and the hesitation it was carved out of.

Poetry

Poems of landscape, memory, and belonging — written from the Salt Range, attentive to the seasons, the household, and the distances between tradition and modernity.

Poem · Nature · 2026

The Lake at Dusk

The surface of a childhood lake becomes a place where memory, distance, and the passage of time meet.
The light goes down the way it always has, unhurried, unconcerned with who is watching— gold folding into grey along the water, the hills drawing their old blue line behind it. I have been gone longer than I lived here, and still the lake does not ask where. It keeps the shape of the evening the way a hand keeps the shape of a bowl. Somewhere a boy is throwing stones that will never reach the far shore. I was that boy. I am still counting the rings before they disappear. Nothing here has changed enough to notice, which is its own kind of mercy— a place that stayed still so I would have somewhere to come back to.
Poem · Landscape · 2025

Salt in the Hills

A meditation on the Salt Range, exploring the relationship between landscape, history, and the marks left by time.
The hills do not remember names, only weight— the weight of feet, of carts, of centuries pressed into whatever passes for soil. Salt rises through the rock like a memory that refuses to be buried, white veins in the red evening, a mineral patience older than any of us. Wind moves through the passes the way it must have moved before there were roads to follow it, before anyone thought to name the wind. I walk here and feel small in the correct proportion— not erased, only reminded that the hills were keeping time before I arrived to ask what time it was.
Poem · Nature · 2025

Before the Streetlights

A recollection of nights when the sky belonged to darkness, stars, and the quietness of an earlier world.
Before the streetlights, the sky came all the way down. We didn't know to call it light pollution— we called it a good night, one with enough stars to lose count on purpose. My grandmother would sit outside past dark, not doing anything, which felt like doing everything. The night had room in it then for silence that wasn't waiting to be filled. Now the sky over that same yard holds maybe a dozen stars, apologetically, between the glow of somebody's porch light and the glow of somebody's screen. I don't say this to complain about progress. I say it because I was there before the light got so loud it drowned out the quiet, ordinary dark.
Poem · Memory · 2025

A Mountain Seen Once

A brief glimpse of a distant mountain becomes an enduring image, questioning why certain moments remain with us.
It was there for the length of a curve in the road, grey-blue, unnamed, gone before the bus finished the turn that revealed it— and somehow it has outlasted places I lived in for years. I don't remember the town before it or the town after. I remember the mountain the way you remember a name you were never told. Maybe permanence isn't about time spent but about the angle of the light when a thing chooses to be seen. The mountain didn't ask to be remembered. It just was, once, entirely. I have visited grander places since, stood in front of things built to be looked at. None of them have followed me home the way that mountain did, uninvited, unbothered, still there.
Poem · Nature · 2024

What the River Keeps

A reflection on rivers as witnesses to generations, carrying fragments of memory long after people have moved on.
The river doesn't keep names either, but it keeps something— the bend where a boat once turned, the bank where a house used to stand before the house left. People move the way water insists on moving: downstream, away, toward somewhere else, while the river stays in place by the simple trick of never stopping. I used to think it forgot everything, carried it out to some larger, indifferent sea. Now I think it keeps a kind of ledger— silt is just memory that settled. Whatever we can't carry with us, the river takes without complaint, holding what our leaving couldn't, and letting the rest run on toward the wide, forgetting sea.
Poem · Family · 2024

The Tree Outside My Grandfather's House

Childhood memories gather around an old tree as a family home slowly disappears into the past.
The tree is taller than the house now, which the house does not seem to mind. It has watched the paint change twice, the door change once, and still hasn't finished growing. I carved nothing into it as a child— I was told not to, and, for once, I listened. It didn't need my initials. It already knew whose hands had climbed it. My grandfather used to sit beneath it in the hour before the heat set in, as if the shade itself were a kind of company that didn't require conversation. The house will likely be sold someday, the way houses are, when the people who filled them have gone on to fill other rooms. The tree, I think, will simply keep standing— the last relative who never had to leave.
Poem · Landscape · 2024

After the Rain

A familiar landscape is transformed by rain, revealing how places can change while still holding their memories.
The street I've walked a thousand times looks unfamiliar for exactly one hour after rain— the dust gone, the color returned to things that had quietly agreed to fade. Even the hills seem to reconsider themselves, sharper at the edges, closer than they were, as if the rain had washed away some agreed-upon distance between us and them. I like this hour because it lies a little— it suggests the place could always look like this, freshly made, uncomplicated, before the dust remembers its job and returns. By evening the ordinary version comes back, and I am glad of it too. Change, even brief, is proof that the place was never as fixed as I assumed.
Poem · Nature · 2023

The Last Quiet Field

A quiet reflection on rural spaces disappearing beneath roads, buildings, and the movement of modern life.
There is one field left that no one has built on, mostly because no one has gotten around to it yet. I go there when I want to remember what the whole valley used to sound like. Nothing dramatic happens in a quiet field. That is, in fact, the entire point of it. Grass moves. A bird decides something. The silence isn't empty—it's simply not for sale. I know what's coming. I've watched it happen to every field before this one— the stakes, the noise, the sudden certainty that quiet was only ever a waiting room. So I go now, before the waiting ends, and stand in what's left of the nothing, trying to memorize a sound that no one will think to record until it's gone.
Poem · Belonging · 2023

Maps of Home

An exploration of home as something carried within us, shaped by places, people, language, and memory.
Home was never only the house— it was the specific slant of afternoon light across a particular wall, a language spoken nowhere else exactly like this. I have left it more than once and found, each time, that I hadn't— that a map of it had folded itself into some drawer I keep carrying. You can leave the streets. You cannot leave the sound of your name said in the voice that first taught you to answer to it. That part of the map has no edges. So when people ask where I'm from, I give them the province, the district, the town— useful, but incomplete, a shorthand for something I keep no other copy of.
Poem · Memory · 2023

Night Without Electricity

A childhood night without electricity opens into a world of stars, conversation, silence, and unexpected closeness.
The night the power failed, no one panicked. Someone found a candle. Someone found a story. My uncle, who never talked much, suddenly had opinions about everything. Outside, the stars did what they always do when nothing competes with them— they simply became visible again, patient, as if they'd been waiting for an opening. We sat in the courtyard longer than we meant to, past the hour we'd normally have scattered to separate rooms and separate screens, because there was, for once, nowhere else worth going. When the lights came back, something in the room changed— not sadly, just quietly, the way a conversation ends when it has, without announcement, said enough.
Stories

Short fiction

Short stories set among small towns and changing households — where family memory meets new machines, and a place is held between what it was and what it is becoming.

Short Story · Literary Fiction · 2026

The Last Ordinary Day

A seemingly unremarkable day takes on a different meaning when its characters realize they will never experience it in quite the same way again.

The morning began the way every morning began in that house: the kettle first, then the radio, then the particular argument about whether the windows should be open or closed. Nobody in the family would later be able to say what was said at breakfast. It hadn't seemed worth remembering at the time.

By midday, the mother had hung the washing in the same order she always hung it — sheets first, along the outer line, so the smaller things could dry in their shade. The father had gone to the shop and come back with the wrong brand of tea, which prompted a complaint that had been made, in one form or another, for eleven years.

It was an ordinary day. That was, in the end, the whole of its significance.

In the evening, the youngest daughter noticed her father leave his cup on the veranda railing instead of carrying it inside, a small carelessness so unlike him that she almost said something. She didn't. There was nothing, that evening, that seemed to require comment.

They would not know, for another three weeks, that this had been the last evening the five of them sat in that courtyard together, in that configuration, in that house. A transfer letter would arrive. A hospital would call. A decision, already made somewhere out of sight, would begin to unfold in ways none of them could have read into the tea, the washing, the cup left carelessly on a railing.

Years later, the daughter would try to reconstruct that day in detail, the way you press on a bruise to see if it still hurts. She could remember the smell of the wrong tea. She could not remember what anyone had said. It occurred to her, finally, that this was the nature of the last ordinary day — it never announces itself. It only waits, patiently, to be recognized afterward, by people who were too busy living it to notice it was the one that mattered.

Short Story · Family Fiction · 2025

The House We Sold

Returning to a childhood home after years away, a daughter confronts the difference between the house she remembers and the place that remains.

She had expected the drive to take longer than it did. Childhood distances, it turned out, were mostly a matter of scale — the town had not grown, she had.

The new owners were kind enough to let her walk through. They had painted the walls a color her mother would have hated and moved the kitchen table to where the bookshelf used to stand. Still, she recognized the house immediately, the way you recognize a voice on the phone before the person says their name.

In the room that had been hers, a boy's bicycle leaned against the wall where her bed used to be. She stood there longer than was polite, trying to locate the exact spot where she'd once measured her height in pencil marks — painted over now, of course, along with everything else.

The courtyard felt smaller than she remembered, which she'd been warned about but hadn't believed. Here was where her grandmother had shelled peas in the evenings. Here was where her brother had broken his arm falling from the wall he'd been told, repeatedly, not to climb.

None of it belonged to her anymore. That was the strange part — not that the house had changed, but that it no longer needed her permission to change. It had a life of its own now, one she wasn't in.

Driving away, she understood something she hadn't been able to name before: the house she remembered and the house that stood on that street were, in fact, two different buildings occupying the same coordinates. One could be sold. The other, it turned out, could not — it had simply moved somewhere she could still visit, but never return to.

Short Story · Childhood Fiction · 2025

The Lake Has No Bottom

A child's mysterious belief about a lake gradually becomes a story about imagination, fear, and the loss of childhood certainty.

Every child in the village learned about the lake before they learned to swim in it. The older children were specific: nobody had ever touched the bottom. Divers had tried, ropes had been lowered, and still no one had found where it ended.

The adults offered explanations — silt, cold currents, an old irrigation channel that confused people's sense of depth — but explanations were no match for a good story, and the lake's mystery had a long head start.

For a while, the boy believed all of it. He imagined a second village beneath the surface, houses with their doors still open, waiting for people who had drowned generations ago and simply kept living down there, quietly, the way people do. He imagined creatures with too many eyes, patient enough to wait a hundred years for someone careless.

He was eleven when his cousin, visiting from the city and unimpressed by local mythology, waded out one afternoon and touched bottom in under four feet of water, not thirty yards from shore.

It should have ended the mystery. Instead, it complicated it. The boy went home unsettled, not because the lake had been explained, but because it had been explained so easily, by someone who hadn't even wanted to know.

He still remembers standing at the edge of that ordinary, shallow water, feeling something he didn't yet have the words for — the particular disappointment of growing older, in which every mystery, sooner or later, turns out to be something you could have waded into all along.

Short Story · Literary Fiction · 2025

The Mountain Behind the Bus Window

A passing view from a bus window becomes an unexpected landmark in the memory of a traveler.

The bus had been travelling for six hours when the mountain appeared. Most of the other passengers were asleep, or pretending to be, which is its own kind of sleep on long journeys.

He had been watching the landscape idly, the way you watch things you don't expect to remember — fields, a river, a line of electricity poles marching toward a horizon that never seemed to get closer. Then the road curved, and for perhaps ninety seconds, a mountain stood directly ahead of the bus, blue-grey, its upper half lost in cloud, close enough to seem enormous and far enough to seem unreal.

He didn't take a photograph. His phone was in his bag, and by the time he considered reaching for it, the road had curved again and the mountain was gone, folded back behind the hills that had been hiding it all along.

He never learned its name. He never returned to that road. And yet, years later, living in a city with no mountains at all, he would find himself thinking of it more often than places he had lived in for a decade — the specific blue of it, the way it had simply been there, uninterested in whether anyone was looking.

He came to think that memory doesn't reward effort so much as suddenness. The places he'd tried hardest to preserve — with photographs, with souvenirs, with deliberate goodbyes — had faded anyway. The mountain, which had asked nothing of him, refused to leave.

Short Story · Family Fiction · 2024

My Father's Postings

A child's memories of repeatedly leaving home reveal the quiet emotional cost of a family's constantly changing addresses.

By the time she was twelve, she had lived in five houses in four cities, and had developed the specific skill of making friends quickly and losing them without visible damage. It was, her mother said, simply what happened to a family that followed a father's postings.

Each new house had its own smell for the first week — paint, or dust, or someone else's cooking still lodged in the walls — before it settled into the ordinary smell of home. Each new school had its own version of the same first day: the teacher's introduction, the classroom's collective stare, the long walk to a seat near the back.

She began, without quite deciding to, collecting small things instead of people — a particular tree outside one school, a neighbor's voice that carried through a shared wall, the exact creak of a gate in a house she'd lived in for fourteen months. These were the things that didn't leave when she did, because she carried them herself.

Her father apologized once, on the drive to yet another new house, for what the moving had cost them. She told him, honestly, that she didn't mind — and mostly, this was true. What she didn't tell him was that she had stopped expecting home to be a place at all. Home, for her, had quietly become a method: notice quickly, attach carefully, remember generously.

It was not the childhood other people had. But she suspected, watching her own children grow up in one house, on one street, that she had gained something they might never need to learn — how to leave, and how to keep the leaving from being loss.

Short Story · Memory · 2024

The Photograph I Don't Have

The absence of a photograph leads a woman to question how much of a family history can survive without being recorded.

The photograph came up at every family gathering, always described in more detail than the last time. Her aunt remembered the exact arrangement — who stood where, who sat, who had been made to move at the last second because the light was wrong. Her uncle remembered the clothes, down to the color of a shawl no one else recalled seeing. Her mother remembered, above all, that her own grandmother had been smiling in it, which mattered to her more than anything else in the frame.

No one had the photograph. It had been lost, or lent, or possibly never developed — the story of its disappearance had almost as many versions as the story of its contents.

She had grown up believing she remembered it too, until one afternoon she realized, with some discomfort, that she couldn't actually picture her great-grandmother's face at all. What she had was a photograph of a photograph — an image built entirely from other people's descriptions, repeated so often it had come to feel like memory.

This unsettled her more than she expected. If a memory could be manufactured this convincingly from nothing but retelling, how much of the rest of her family's history was built the same way — sincere, detailed, and entirely secondhand?

She stopped asking about the photograph after that, not because she'd lost interest, but because she'd begun to suspect that the photograph's real value had never been in what it showed. It was in what it had given the family permission to imagine together, for thirty years, in its absence.

Short Story · Family Fiction · 2024

When the Lights Went Out

During an unexpected power outage, a family temporarily steps away from their screens and rediscovers the conversations they had forgotten how to have.

The outage lasted four hours, which was unremarkable by the standards of that particular summer. What was remarkable was what happened inside the house during it.

For the first twenty minutes, everyone simply waited, the way people wait for a delayed film to resume — phones held up hopefully, half-charged, useless without a signal worth using. The children complained. The father checked his phone out of habit, twice, before remembering there was nothing to check.

Then the grandmother, seated by the window for the breeze, began telling a story about her own childhood that none of them had heard before — a flood, a lost dog, an uncle who had once outrun a wild boar and never let anyone forget it. One story invited another. The mother remembered an incident from her wedding that made everyone laugh in a way the family hadn't laughed together in months.

By the time the electricity returned, no one moved to switch anything back on immediately. The room sat for a moment in the new, humming light, as if deciding whether it wanted it.

Later, the father would half-joke that they should turn the power off on purpose, once a month, just to see what else they'd forgotten they had. No one took him up on it. But for a while afterward, dinner lasted a little longer than usual, and someone always seemed to have one more story left to tell.

Short Story · Place & Landscape · 2023

The Salt Road

A journey through the Salt Range becomes an encounter with stories, landscapes, and histories hidden beneath an ordinary road.

The road through the Salt Range had never struck him as anything more than a route — a way of getting from one ordinary place to another, distinguished mostly by its potholes and the heat that pressed down on it by midday.

It was the driver, an older man who had made the same trip for thirty years, who first mentioned the shrine half-buried near the third bend, and the well beyond it that no longer held water but had, apparently, once served an entire caravan route. He spoke of it the way people speak of things they've stopped finding remarkable — factually, without embellishment, the way you'd mention a landmark on a road you no longer really see.

At a tea stall further along, an old man added more: a story of a settlement that had once stood where there was now only a flat stretch of scrubland, abandoned after a drought two generations back. Nothing marked the place. No sign, no ruin. Only the story, passed from one driver, one tea stall, to the next.

By the end of the journey, the road had stopped feeling like a road at all. It felt more like a sentence someone had been writing for centuries, one traveler's memory added to the next, none of it recorded anywhere but in the retelling.

He has driven that road many times since. He no longer sees it as a route between two points. He sees it as something closer to a ledger — of settlements, of droughts, of caravans, of ordinary people whose only monument is a story still being told at a tea stall, to whoever happens to be passing through.

Short Story · Literary Fiction · 2023

The House That Remembered

Told through the presence of an old family house, the story follows generations of departures, returns, celebrations, and loss.

The house had outlived three generations by the time it stood empty. It had seen a wedding held in its courtyard under a canopy that no longer exists, a birth attended by a midwife whose name only the eldest living relative could still recall, and a funeral so large the street outside had to be closed for the afternoon.

A pencil mark on the kitchen doorframe recorded a child's height at seven, at nine, at eleven, and then stopped — the child had grown up and moved to the city, as children in that family generally did. A crack in the courtyard wall, patched twice, still ran in roughly the same place it always had, indifferent to whoever had tried to erase it.

By the time the last of the family left, the house had become mostly quiet — not empty, exactly, but reduced to holding what could no longer be added to. The furniture went first, then the smaller things, until only the walls remained to do the remembering.

A cousin, visiting years later before the sale was finalized, walked through each room slowly, running a hand along the same doorframe, the same wall. She couldn't have said what she was looking for. Perhaps only confirmation that the house had, in fact, held what she remembered — that it hadn't simply imagined a family, the way a family sometimes imagines a house.

It had. The marks were still there, faint but legible, in a language only the family had ever really spoken.

Short Story · Technology & Human Life · 2023

The Signal

In a world where everyone is constantly connected, a broken signal forces one person to confront a loneliness that technology cannot solve.

She had over three hundred contacts and rarely felt she had anyone to call. The apartment stayed lit blue most evenings, notifications arriving in a steady, reassuring rhythm that she had come to mistake, without quite noticing, for company.

The outage, when it came, lasted only six hours — a fault at the local exchange, the message said later, apologetically. For the first hour, she found herself picking up her phone out of habit, an unconscious twitch toward a screen that had nothing to offer her.

By the second hour, restless, she stepped out onto the landing, where she found a neighbor doing much the same thing — leaning against the railing, looking, for lack of anything better to look at, at the street below.

They had lived on the same floor for two years and exchanged, in that time, perhaps a dozen words. That evening, with nothing else competing for their attention, they talked for nearly an hour — about nothing important, about the heat, about a stray cat that had adopted the stairwell. It was, she realized afterward, the longest conversation she'd had with an actual, physically present person in longer than she wanted to admit.

When the signal returned, her phone buzzed insistently, three hours of notifications arriving all at once. She looked at it for a moment, then set it face-down on the railing and stayed outside a while longer, talking to the one person, that evening, who hadn't required a signal at all.
